specPoints.text: CORE PRACTICAL 5 Investigation of the rates of hydrolysis of some halogenoalkanes.

primer.text: Three halogenoalkanes, three stop-watches, one verdict. This core practical times the hydrolysis of chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes with acidified silver nitrate, pairing each precipitate colour with its halide and reading the finishing order straight off the carbon-halogen bond enthalpies.

lessons.title: Core Practical 5: timing the halide race
lessons.opening: Halogenoalkanes surrender their halogen to aqueous alkali at rates set by the carbon-halogen bond. This core practical races a chloroalkane, a bromoalkane and an iodoalkane side by side, using acidified silver nitrate to time the precipitates and reading the finishing order as bond enthalpy.
keyPoints: Halogenoalkanes are hydrolysed by aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide, replacing the halogen with OH.
The reaction is slow at room temperature, so the mixtures are warmed in a water bath.
The rate depends on the halogen: stronger carbon-halogen bonds mean slower hydrolysis, ranking C-F above C-Cl above C-Br above C-I in strength.
Acidified silver nitrate in ethanol times the hydrolysis, as halide ions released form precipitates of AgCl, AgBr and AgI.
The yellow iodide precipitate appears first and the white chloride last, because the C-I bond is weakest and the C-Cl strongest.

low.restatement: Three tubes, three halogenoalkanes, one stop-watch each: whichever precipitate appears first belongs to the weakest carbon-halogen bond, and the finishing order is iodide, then bromide, then chloride.
low.analogy: Three locks of different stubbornness opened by the same key: the flimsiest lock (C-I) opens first and the toughest (C-Cl) keeps the door shut longest.
low.examPointer: Quote the bond-strength ladder and pair each precipitate colour with its halide when describing the experiment.

medium.restatement: Hydroxide out-competes water as the nucleophile because it carries a full negative charge while water's oxygen only carries a partial one, so the alkali route is much faster; within the alkali route, bond enthalpy is the clock - each mole of C-X bonds broken costs a fixed enthalpy, and the cheapest bond yields its halide ion soonest.
medium.analogy: Breaking ropes of different thickness with the same pull: the thin rope (C-I) parts first and the thick one (C-Cl) resists longest.
medium.examPointer: Explain the nucleophile charge comparison when a question contrasts the water and alkali routes.

check.stem: Which reagent hydrolyses halogenoalkanes in this core practical?

options.text: Aqueous sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide
options.explanation: The aqueous alkali supplies hydroxide ions that replace the halogen.

options.text: Dry sodium carbonate
options.explanation: Carbonate solution is for washing organic layers, not hydrolysis.

options.text: Concentrated phosphoric acid
options.explanation: That dehydrates alcohols, unrelated here.

options.text: Molten potassium dichromate
options.explanation: Dichromate oxidises alcohols, not halogenoalkane hydrolysis.

check.stem: The rate of hydrolysis decreases in the order

options.text: Iodoalkane fastest, then bromoalkane, then chloroalkane
options.explanation: Bond enthalpy rises from C-I to C-Cl, so the iodide reaction is quickest.

options.text: Chloroalkane fastest, then bromoalkane, then iodoalkane
options.explanation: That reverses the bond enthalpy logic.

options.text: All three react at identical rates
options.explanation: The practical exists precisely because the rates differ.

options.text: Fluoroalkane fastest of all
options.explanation: Fluoroalkanes carry the strongest bond and barely react at all.

check.stem: Acidified silver nitrate is used to time the reactions because

options.text: Halide ions released by hydrolysis form precipitates with silver ions, whose appearance can be timed
options.explanation: The precipitate's arrival is the visible clock for the invisible bond breakage.

options.text: Silver nitrate catalyses the hydrolysis directly
options.explanation: The nitrate solution detects halide ions; it does not speed the hydrolysis.

options.text: Silver ions are the nucleophile replacing the halogen
options.explanation: Hydroxide is the nucleophile in the hydrolysis itself.

options.text: The acid dissolves the halogenoalkane instantly
options.explanation: The ethanol solvent dissolves the substrate; the silver is the detector.

options.text: White for chloride, cream for bromide and yellow for iodide
options.explanation: Each silver halide carries its signature colour as it forms.

options.text: Yellow for chloride, white for iodide
options.explanation: The pairing is reversed for those two.

options.text: All three precipitates are white
options.explanation: Only the chloride precipitate is white.

options.text: Blue, green and orange
options.explanation: Those colours belong to transition-metal chemistry.

check.stem: Why is hydroxide a better nucleophile than water in this reaction?

options.text: The hydroxide ion carries a full negative charge while water's oxygen carries only a partial one
options.explanation: Full charge means stronger attack on the electron-poor carbon, so substitution runs faster.

options.text: Hydroxide is lighter than water
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant to nucleophilicity here.

options.text: Water cannot dissolve halogenoalkanes at all
options.explanation: The ethanol cosolvent handles solubility; the charge comparison is the real answer.

options.text: Hydroxide is a stronger acid than water
options.explanation: Hydroxide is a base, not an acid.

check.stem: State the bond enthalpy ordering for the carbon-halogen bonds.
check.modelAnswer: Bond enthalpy falls in the order C-F, then C-Cl, then C-Br, then C-I, so the C-I bond breaks most easily.

check.stem: State the conditions used to run the three hydrolysis reactions.
check.modelAnswer: Test tubes in a 50 degree water bath hold ethanol with acidified silver nitrate, and a few drops of each halogenoalkane start the timed reactions.

check.stem: Explain why the yellow precipitate forms fastest in the hydrolysis race.
check.modelAnswer: The yellow precipitate signals iodide ions, released by breaking the C-I bond, whose lowest bond enthalpy of the series makes it the easiest to break and therefore the fastest halide to appear.

check.stem: A fourth tube contains a fluoroalkane. Predict the observation over the practical's timescale and justify it from bond enthalpy.
check.modelAnswer: No precipitate forms, because the C-F bond has the highest bond enthalpy of the series and fluoroalkanes do not hydrolyse under these conditions, so no fluoride ions ever reach the silver nitrate.

glossary.definition: Reaction splitting a molecule by water-derived nucleophile attack; here OH replaces the halogen of a halogenoalkane.
An electron-pair donor that attacks an electron-poor carbon, such as hydroxide or water.
The energy needed to break a bond; the C-X bond's value sets the hydrolysis rate for each halogen.
